verses.translation_literal: To the choirmaster, a psalm, of David.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the choirmaster: a psalm, set in David's name.
verses.directors_commentary: This is a heading, not part of the prayer, and the Hebrew numbering counts it as a verse; the KJV treats it as an unnumbered title (its 'verse 0'), which is why every verse of the psalm in the KJV runs two behind the Hebrew. 'Of David' (ledavid) uses the little preposition le-, which can mean 'by', 'for' or 'belonging to' David; the KJV's 'A Psalm of David' picks one and hides the others. The word 'choirmaster' (lamnatzeach) is the KJV's 'chief Musician'. It comes from a root meaning 'to excel' or 'to lead', and its exact sense is unknown; the Targum reads it as 'to praise'. Treat it as a stage direction: this private cry was handed over to the temple's musicians, so a personal confession became the community's song.

philological_notes.note: Traditionally 'to the choirmaster/leader'. The root ntzch means 'to be preeminent, to lead', and the participle names the one who directs the performance. The Targum instead reads the word as 'to praise' (leshabacha tushbachta).

verses.translation_literal: In the coming to him of Nathan the prophet, as he had come to Bathsheba.
verses.translation_dramatic: It was the day Nathan the prophet came to him, after the king had gone in to Bathsheba.
verses.directors_commentary: The second line of the heading gives the psalm its occasion: the confrontation of 2 Samuel 12, when Nathan told David the story of the stolen lamb. Two different verbs of 'coming' (bo') are set side by side: Nathan 'came to him', and David 'came to Bathsheba'. The Hebrew idiom for sexual union is simply 'to come in to' a woman, so the KJV's 'after he had gone in to Bath-sheba' is a faithful, if discreet, rendering; the Targum is blunter, 'when he had lain with Bathsheba'. Note that the verb tenses differ: Nathan's coming is an infinitive ('in the coming'), David's a completed act ('had come'), so Nathan's visit is the present moment and David's sin lies already behind it. The headings of the Psalms were transmitted with the text but are not part of the prayer itself; Radak adds that the psalm was spoken after Nathan had gone home, and was not the confession he gave to Nathan.

philological_notes.note: 'As he had come to Bathsheba': the idiom 'to come to/in to' a woman is a standard euphemism for intercourse. The Targum spells it out ('when he had lain with Bathsheba').

verses.translation_literal: Show me favor, O God, according to your covenant loyalty; according to the abundance of your compassion wipe out my transgressions.
verses.translation_dramatic: Be gracious to me, O God. Not by what I have earned, but by your own faithful love; by the sheer weight of your mercies, wipe away my rebellions.
verses.directors_commentary: The prayer opens with a plea for a favor nobody can demand. The verb chanan means to show grace to someone with no claim on it, so the KJV's 'Have mercy' blurs it with the other word in the line, rachamim, which the KJV renders 'tender mercies'; the Hebrew asks for favor first, then compassion, then pardon. Chesed, 'covenant loyalty', is what the KJV flattens into the Victorian coinage 'lovingkindness': it is the loyalty that a stronger party owes because he has sworn it. David is not appealing to his merit, but to God's own record, as Radak says: 'not according to my deeds'. Rachamim is plural of the word for the womb, rechem, and means the feeling a mother has for the child she carried. 'Wipe out' (mechah) is the vocabulary of erasing a written record, a clay tablet wiped smooth or a scroll washed clean; the KJV's 'blot out' keeps the image. 'Transgressions' (pesha') is the strongest of the three words for sin used in these verses: rebellion, a breach against a lord. Its plural leads Ibn Ezra and Radak to say both Bathsheba and Uriah are meant. Note the three-way pairing: chesed, rachamim, and, in v. 6, justice; Malbim reads the three as the three grounds on which David asks forgiveness.

philological_notes.note: 'Show me favor/grace': a plea for what the speaker has no claim to. The KJV's 'Have mercy' merges it with rachamim in the next line.
Covenant loyalty, the faithfulness a stronger party owes to a weaker one by oath; not simply 'kindness'.
Rebellion, breach against a lord, the strongest of the three sin-words in vv. 3-11; plural because the act of adultery and the killing of Uriah are both in view.

verses.translation_literal: Multiply! wash me from my iniquity, and from my sin cleanse me.
verses.translation_dramatic: Again, and again, and again. Scrub me. The stain is not on the surface; it has gone down into the weave of me. Wash me out of my crookedness, and from the sin that clings to me, make me clean.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a laundry cry. The verb כבס is the one used for washing cloth, the heavy work of treading and beating garments clean, and the speaker treats his guilt as a stain that has sunk into the fabric. Radak says as much: guilt on the soul is like a spot on a garment. Play it as someone who knows that one rinse will not do.

The KJV 'wash me throughly' is neat but hides a textual wrinkle. The consonants written in the text (the Ketiv) are הרבה, harbeh, 'much, thoroughly', an adverb, and the KJV follows that. The reading the tradition says aloud (the Qere) is הֶרֶב, herev, a Hiphil imperative, 'multiply!'. Radak notes that the two are the same in sense, and Ibn Ezra and Meiri give both options. On the Qere, the speaker commands God to multiply the washing, or, as Radak and Meiri have it, to multiply his mercy. Either way the point is excess: more than one cleansing. The two verbs also pair up, 'wash' for the cloth, 'cleanse' (טהר) for ritual purity, so the speaker asks for both clean linen and a clean status before God. The KJV flattens 'iniquity' and 'sin' into synonyms; עָוֺן is the crookedness or twisted deed with its guilt, חַטָּאת the missing of the mark.

philological_notes.note: The Qere is a Hiphil imperative, 'multiply!', the written Ketiv הרבה is an adverb, 'much, thoroughly'. The KJV 'throughly' follows the Ketiv. With the Qere the sense is 'do the washing again and again', or 'multiply your mercy and wash me'. Both readings give the same stress on thoroughness.

The verb for laundering cloth, here with the intensive (Piel) stem, 'wash me thoroughly'. It makes guilt a stain in the fabric of the person, as Radak says: iniquity in the soul is like a spot on a garment.

verses.translation_literal: For my transgressions I myself know, and my sin is before me continually.
verses.translation_dramatic: Because I know them, my rebellions: I, I know them. And my sin stands in front of me, always, wherever I turn.
verses.directors_commentary: The 'for' (ki) gives the reason for the plea: nothing to be uncovered, because the sinner is not hiding anything. The pronoun is explicit, 'I myself', unneeded in Hebrew with this verb: it is the confession of someone who will not shift the blame, which Meiri sets against Cain's 'Am I my brother's keeper?'. The KJV's 'I acknowledge' is a legal word, for what the Hebrew says is simply 'I know'. The second line is a picture: the sin is 'before me', negdi, literally 'in front of me, opposite me', as a person might stand facing a judge or a man in front of a mirror; Rashi says it is because he regrets it and worries over it that it seems to be always before him. 'Continually' (tamid) is the same word used for the daily offering that was never allowed to lapse, so the sin has become a perpetual fixture.

philological_notes.note: 'I know': the KJV's 'acknowledge' makes it a legal confession; the Hebrew is the plain verb of knowing, here meaning to recognize and not deny.
'In front of me, opposite me': the sin faces him like an accuser.

verses.translation_literal: To you, to your being alone, I have sinned, and the evil in your eyes I have done, so that you may be in the right in your speaking, [and] be clear in your judging.
verses.translation_dramatic: Against you, you alone, I have sinned. It was done under your eyes, the evil, and I did it. Let no one say you spoke unjustly. When you speak, you are in the right; when you judge, your hands are clean.
verses.directors_commentary:
The line is blunt, and the actor should not rush it. 'To you alone I have sinned' does not deny that other people were hurt; the psalm's own heading ties it to Bathsheba and Uriah. The traditional commentators ask why only God. Rashi: because God had forbidden the act, so the offence is against the commandment. Radak: because the deeds were done in secret and nobody knew the reasons behind them, so God alone knew. Meiri: because the sin of a man against another needs reconciling and restitution, and this one has become a matter between the man and God. Metzudat David adds that if the offended party had been a man, forgiveness would be his to give, so only God can grant it here.

The second half is a famous difficulty. The Hebrew 'so that' (לְמַעַן) can be read as purpose or as result. The KJV 'that thou mightest be justified' keeps the purpose and leaves it unexplained. Rashi gives two readings: the test David failed (God had put him to the test and he did not pass, so that God would be proved right rather than he); or, if God forgives him, God is vindicated before sinners who refuse to repent, who could otherwise say that repenting did them no good. Meiri reads it as 'if you punish me, it is all just', so that any punishment would show God righteous. Radak reads 'you will bear my sin, as you said to Moses'. The KJV also gives 'be clear' for תִּזְכֶּה, which means to be pure or innocent; the sense is that God is not open to any charge. The verb pair 'be in the right' and 'be pure' is a courtroom pair: the speaker takes the dock and lets the judge's verdict stand. The KJV 'done this evil' adds 'this' (in italics in the KJV itself); the Hebrew has 'the evil in your eyes', the evil as you see it.

philological_notes.note: 'Your being alone': the noun בַּד, 'part, separation', with the preposition and suffix. The Hebrew is more emphatic than the English 'only'. The double 'to you, to you alone' puts the weight on God as the only party of the offence.

'So that, in order that'. Meiri observes that it can stand for a cause, as in Hosea 8:4, not only a purpose. Most translators keep it as purpose, which is why the verse sounds as if the sin served God's vindication.
'You will be in the right', a courtroom word: to be found just in a dispute. Paired with תִּזְכֶּה 'you will be clear, pure'. God is both the judge and the party whose word is on trial.

token_glosses.gloss: you may be in the right

verses.translation_literal: Look, in iniquity I was brought forth in labor, and in sin my mother conceived me.
verses.translation_dramatic: Look at me: I was born into crookedness, and my mother warmed me into being in sin.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the verse behind the Christian doctrine of original sin, but nothing in the Hebrew demands it, and the Jewish commentators do not read it that way. 'Look' (hen) opens a plea of weakness rather than a statement of doctrine: this is how I am made. The verb chol, here chololti, means 'to writhe, to be in labor', so 'brought forth' captures the birth pangs that 'shapen' in the KJV (from the Vulgate's 'conceptus') loses. The second verb is more startling: yechematni is from a root that means 'to be hot' (Rashi compares the flock that 'became hot' in Genesis 30:38), and it is the warmth of animals in heat; 'conceive' is the KJV's polite synonym. Radak says that the human being is made out of a drop of seed in the heat of intercourse, so that desire is built into the material; Meiri reads the verse as hyperbole, 'sinner from the womb', like Isaiah 48:8; Metzudat David says the impulse to evil was strong in him. Even the Hebrew 'in sin' does not make the mother sinful: the preposition says the circumstances of the beginning were marked by the human desire, not that conception was a sin. Compare the Rabbinic reading in Radak: 'even the most pious of the pious has some side of iniquity'.

philological_notes.note: 'I was brought forth in labor': a Polal of chul, 'to writhe, to travail', used also in Isaiah 51:2. The KJV's 'shapen' is a Vulgate-influenced loose translation.
'Became hot with me', the warmth of animals in heat, as in Genesis 30:38; the KJV's 'conceive' covers a verb that is physical and bodily.

token_glosses.gloss: I was brought forth in labor
she conceived me (became warm with me)

verses.translation_literal: Look, truth you desire in the plastered-over places, and in a secret place wisdom you make me know.
verses.translation_dramatic: And yet, look: you want truth in the hidden depths. In the secret place of me, you teach me wisdom.
verses.directors_commentary: The second 'look' (hen) turns the argument: the God who sees where the sin began also looks for truth in the same hidden place. The Hebrew word 'truth' is emet, faithfulness, reliability, as well as the opposite of a lie; the KJV's 'truth' works but loses the 'steadfastness' that links to the 'steadfast spirit' of v. 12. The difficult word is tuchot, which occurs only here and in Job 38:36 ('who put wisdom in the tuchot?'). The tradition says it is the kidneys 'covered in fat' (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Metzudat Zion), the seat of conscience in ancient Hebrew anatomy, from tuach 'to smear over'; the KJV's 'inward parts' follows. The parallel 'secret place' (satum) means sealed, closed up, hidden. Wisdom (chokhmah) is here a gift taught in secret, not a quality that a person already has. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri disagree on what the verse means: whether it is a statement that his faith did not waver, an excuse, or a hope that God will teach him.

philological_notes.note: A rare word, only here and Job 38:36. Rashi and Ibn Ezra take it as the kidneys, 'covered with fat', from the root 'to smear over'; Rashi also offers 'extent'. Context favors 'inner parts'.
Faithfulness, firmness, truth; the same root as 'amen'.

verses.translation_literal: You will un-sin me with hyssop, and I will be clean; you will wash me, and more than snow I will be white.
verses.translation_dramatic: Take the hyssop to me, and I shall be clean. Wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow.
verses.directors_commentary: Now the picture is the temple. Hyssop is a small, bushy herb whose leafy stems were used as a brush to sprinkle the blood and water of purification: on a person cured of skin disease (Leviticus 14:4) or on one defiled by contact with the dead (Numbers 19:6), as Rashi observes. The verb tchatteni is the strangest word in the verse: it is a Piel of chata', 'to sin', and so means literally 'to de-sin' me, to take the sin off. The KJV's 'purge' hides the pun, which the Hebrew makes on the same word that names the offense. The verb forms are imperfects, expressing a wish, not a plain future; the KJV's 'and I shall be clean' is therefore too confident. Snow is the whitest thing an inhabitant of the Judean hills could imagine; and the verb alvin, 'I will be white', is intransitive, as Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri each observe. Ibn Ezra and Radak note that the speaker likens sin to a skin disease, which would make hyssop the right remedy.

philological_notes.note: Piel of chata', 'to sin': a privative, 'to remove sin from', 'to un-sin'. The KJV's 'purge' loses the wordplay.
Hyssop, a leafy herb used as a sprinkler in purification rites (Lev 14:4, Num 19:6).
'I will be white': a form that is intransitive, as in Joel 1:7 'their branches turned white'.

verses.translation_literal: You will make me hear joy and gladness; let the bones you crushed rejoice.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let me hear laughter again, joy and gladness. Let the bones you crushed dance.
verses.directors_commentary: The senses shift from sight to sound. David asks to 'hear' joy, that is, to hear the word of forgiveness. Rashi and Radak both take it as the announcement of pardon, in Radak's reading by a prophet. The KJV's 'Make me to hear' is accurate; the Hebrew is causative. The most striking image is the bones. In Hebrew thought the bones are the frame of the whole person, and they can ache or shake with terror or illness (Psalm 6:3, 32:3); 'crushed' (dikita) is the same strong verb for grinding to powder, which the KJV softens to 'broken'. The agent is God: it was the Lord who crushed him, as Rashi says, 'when you were angry with me'. Radak adds the old claim that good news fattens the bones. Malbim sees the entire psalm as David as a person with skin disease, shut outside the camp in torn clothes, restored to community.

philological_notes.note: 'Bones you crushed': the bones stand for the whole body, and the crushing is God's doing, as Rashi says, in his anger. The KJV's 'broken' is weaker.
A causative: 'make me hear'; the joy is a message that is heard, namely forgiveness.

verses.translation_literal: Hide your face from my sins, and all my iniquities wipe out.
verses.translation_dramatic: Turn your face away from my sins. And all my guilt, every last stroke of it, wipe out.
verses.directors_commentary: A prayer that sounds strange to modern ears: the speaker has asked God to see him in v. 3, and now asks him to look away. Elsewhere in the Psalms the 'hidden face' of God is a threat (Psalm 30:7); here it is a mercy, for the thing the face must not look at is the sin. Ibn Ezra says it is a figure, 'that he not see the anger of the Lord'; Meiri and Radak say it means 'do not remember and do not punish'. The verse closes by returning to the verb of v. 3, 'wipe out' (mechah), now with 'all' my iniquities in the plural: the confession has moved from the single act to the whole account. The KJV's 'blot out all mine iniquities' is accurate, but note that 'iniquities' (avonot) is the plural of the twisting-word of v. 4. The sequence 'transgressions, iniquity, sin' keeps the three Hebrew sin-words together through the prayer.

philological_notes.note: 'Hide your face': a figure for not looking at, not remembering and not punishing the sin; the opposite of the hidden face of anger.

verses.translation_literal: A pure heart create for me, O God, and a steadfast spirit renew within me.
verses.translation_dramatic: Make a clean heart in me, O God, a heart made new, and set a steady spirit within me again.
verses.directors_commentary: The turning-point of the psalm. The verb bara', 'create', is used in the Bible almost only with God as its subject, and with something new that has not existed before: the same word as Genesis 1:1. So the KJV's 'Create in me' is exact; it is the request not for repair but for a new making. The 'heart' (lev) is the seat of thought and will rather than of feeling, so a 'pure heart' is a clear, undivided mind. 'Right spirit' in the KJV translates ruach nakhon, a 'steadfast, firmly set' spirit: nakhon is the participle of the verb 'to be firm' (kun), used for a house standing on its foundation, so the contrast is a spirit that sways. 'Renew' (chadesh) is the verb for rebuilding a city or restoring a worn garment. Malbim notes the difference between the two: the heart must be created, because the body's desires are inborn, but the spirit only needs renewing, as it was originally good. The prayer addresses God as 'Elohim', the name of God as Creator, which fits the verb.

philological_notes.note: 'Create': a verb used in the Bible of divine action only; the request is for a new making, not a repair.
'Steadfast, firmly set', passive participle of kun, 'to be established'; the KJV's 'right' is a weaker translation.

verses.translation_literal: Do not cast me from before your face, and the spirit of your holiness do not take from me.
verses.translation_dramatic: Do not throw me out of your sight. Do not send me away from the light of your face. And the breath of your holiness, that breath that has been mine, do not take it from me now.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two negative commands, short and symmetrical, spoken by someone who knows he deserves the opposite. The verb 'cast' is physical: this is what one does with rubbish, or with a person driven out of the household or the sanctuary. 'From before your face' is the language of the court and of the temple: to stand before the king's face is to have access, and to be cast from it is to be exiled from favour. Every ancient listener knew that a king's face could be a blessing or a death sentence.

The KJV 'thy holy spirit' makes this sound like a later doctrine. The Hebrew is 'the spirit of your holiness', and it occurs in the Bible only here and in Isaiah 63. Rashi, Radak and Meiri read it as the inspiration that gave David his songs; the Targum says outright 'the spirit of prophecy of your holiness'. So the fear is not abstract: it is the fear of losing the voice in which he speaks to God. Note also the numbering: in the Hebrew text the psalm's heading is verse 1, so this verse is 13 where the KJV counts it as 11.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'spirit of your holiness', with the noun 'holiness' in the construct and the suffix on it. It is rare in the Hebrew Bible (compare Isa 63:10-11), and the medieval commentators read it as inspiration or prophecy rather than as a person.
'Cast, hurl', the verb used for throwing an object away. The jussive with 'al makes a strong prohibition, almost a cry.

verses.translation_literal: Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and a willing spirit will sustain me.
verses.translation_dramatic: Give me back the joy I had when you saved me. Give it back, and let a willing spirit, a spirit that gives itself freely, hold me up when I have no strength of my own.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verb 'restore' (hashivah) is the same root as 'return' that will appear in verse 15: the whole second half of the psalm turns on shuv. The joy he asks for was once his, and he knows exactly what its loss feels like. Note the grammar that the KJV hides: 'sustain' is a feminine verb, 'it will sustain me', so the willing spirit is the one doing the holding. KJV 'uphold me with thy free spirit' turns the subject into a tool.

The word nadiv carries three shades, all of them in the commentators: willing (Radak, the voluntary song), generous (Metzudat Zion), and noble or princely (Rashi). English 'free', as in KJV, hears only the last of these. Ibn Ezra adds that the purpose of the sustaining is 'to give oneself willingly until I teach', which links this verse to the next.

philological_notes.note: 'The joy of your salvation': either the joy that comes from your saving act or the joy you feel in saving. The doubling of the sin in sason is itself expressive.
A 'willing' or 'generous' spirit; the root also gives the freewill offering (nedava) and the noble (nadiv). Rashi reads nobility, Radak the willing spirit that offers songs.
From the verb for leaning on or supporting; the feminine form shows the spirit as the one that sustains.

verses.translation_literal: I will teach transgressors your ways, and sinners to you will return.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then I will teach them, the ones who broke away, the ones who walked off your road. I will show them your ways, and the sinners will turn and come back to you.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verb is a cohortative: 'let me teach', 'I will teach', a vow made as the price of forgiveness. Rashi sees the logic: they will learn from me and return, if they see that you forgave me. Radak and Meiri say the same in other words: no one will despair of repentance when they see how great a sin was pardoned. The verse stages the psalmist as a living example.

The two nouns are not synonyms. 'Transgressors' (poshe'im) are those who rebel; 'sinners' (chata'im) are those who miss the mark. Ibn Ezra matches them to the words 'my transgressions' and 'my sin' earlier in the psalm. Malbim, later, divides them: the rebels need teaching, the sinners of appetite need only an example. The KJV 'shall be converted' sounds like evangelism; the Hebrew is the plain verb 'return', yashuvu, with 'to you' placed ahead of it for emphasis.

philological_notes.note: Those who rebel, break with an authority. Ibn Ezra links the word to 'my transgressions' earlier in the psalm; Malbim reads it as sin out of defiance rather than appetite.
'Return', the same root as 'restore' in the previous verse (hashivah); the psalm's turning point is built on this word.

verses.translation_literal: Deliver me from bloods, O God, God of my salvation; my tongue will ring out your righteousness.
verses.translation_dramatic: Pull me out of the blood. Out of the bloodshed, O God, my God who saves me. And then my tongue will sing, it will cry aloud, and what it sings will be your righteousness.
verses.directors_commentary:
'Bloods' is a plural in the Hebrew, damim, and it is the ordinary biblical word for bloodshed and blood-guilt: the blood that cries out from the ground. The KJV 'bloodguiltiness' is a fair guess at the idiom but it makes one abstract noun out of a raw image. Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri all tie it to the death of Uriah, which is the story the psalm's heading points to; the verse itself names no one. Rashi reads the plea as: do not let me die by the sword as Uriah did. Radak reads it as: do not punish me for his blood. Ibn Ezra adds that the king did not order the killing but only placed Uriah in danger.

The address 'O God, God of my salvation' piles up the divine name in a way that sounds like a man gripping a rope. The verb tranen is a ringing cry of joy, not quiet singing; KJV 'sing aloud' gets this. 'Your righteousness' here is God's saving justice, not only a legal verdict.

philological_notes.note: Plural of 'blood', used for shed blood and the guilt of it. Radak remarks that the word occurs in both singular and plural.
Piel of the root for a ringing shout of joy; it is the sound of triumph and thanks, not a murmured hymn.
God's righteousness, in the sense of his faithful, saving justice. Malbim distinguishes it from 'judgment' as a higher mercy.

verses.translation_literal: My Lord, my lips you will open, and my mouth will declare your praise.
verses.translation_dramatic: Lord, open my lips. They are shut, they are sealed with shame. Open them, and my mouth will tell out your praise.
verses.directors_commentary:
This line is still said in the daily Jewish prayer, spoken at the start of the Amidah, which shows how deeply it entered liturgy. In the psalm it is a confession of silence: a man who cannot speak. The address is Adonai, 'my Lord', not the name YHWH, so the dramatic layer says 'Lord' as a plain form of address.

The verb is an imperfect, and the KJV 'open thou' makes it an order. Literally it is 'you will open', a plea that sounds like trust. Rashi reads it as a request for forgiveness that gives him 'an opening of the mouth'. Radak reads it as the return of the spirit that put songs on his tongue. The mouth and the lips are the two halves of speech: the lips open, the mouth declares. In a world where praise is spoken aloud before an audience, silence is a kind of disgrace.

philological_notes.note: 'You will open': an imperfect used as a plea. Rashi hears the idea of an 'opening of the mouth' (pitchon peh), the right to speak that forgiveness gives.

verses.translation_literal: For not you-desire sacrifice, and-I-would-give [it]; burnt-offering not you-are-pleased-with.
verses.translation_dramatic: You take no joy in sacrifice, or I would bring it. I would lay it on the altar this very hour. But the burnt offering, rising in its smoke, does not please you.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the hinge of the psalm, and the speaker says it without bitterness. He is not sneering at the altar; he has looked at it and found it closed to him. The cohortative "I would give" (we'etenah) is a man offering what he has: if a bull could buy back what he has done, he would drive it to the sanctuary himself. Ancient worshippers did exactly that, since sacrifice was the normal currency of repentance and a bull or lamb cost real wealth. The speaker's point is that for this sin the currency is not accepted. Rashi, Radak and Meiri in the packet all read it so: the sacrificial system provides for inadvertent sin, and a deliberate wrong has no offering to cover it, only a broken heart (the next verse).

The English versions blur the shape of the line. The Hebrew sets two near-synonyms in parallel, chafetz ("to take delight in, to want") and ratzah ("to be pleased with, to accept favourably"), one over sacrifice (zevach, the shared meal-offering) and one over the burnt offering ('olah, the whole offering that goes up entirely in smoke). The KJV renders "For thou desirest not sacrifice; else would I give it: thou delightest not in burnt offering." It keeps two different verbs, but "delightest" and "desirest" are close enough to hide that this is one idea said twice. The ASV swaps the distribution: "thou delightest not in sacrifice … thou hast no pleasure in burnt-offering," and the BBE shifts again to "desire … delight." Each version hands the same two Hebrew verbs different English words, so the repetition the poet built is lost. YLT comes nearest by turning ratzah into the technical "acceptest." The KJV's "else would I give it" also turns a single clause into a separate sentence with a semicolon; the Hebrew runs straight on with "and I would give." Say it quickly and flatly, as a man who has already done the arithmetic.

philological_notes.note: To take pleasure in, to want, to desire. It is the language of the heart's inclination, not of formal rule. It is parallel here with tirtzeh, 'you are pleased with', so the line says one thing twice: God does not want this.
First-person cohortative of 'to give', with the added ה: 'and I would give (it)'. It expresses willingness. Metzudat Zion links it to the sense of a gift or payment.

The burnt offering, 'that which goes up': the whole animal is burned and rises in smoke. The word comes from the root 'to go up'. Naming it after zevach, the shared offering, makes the pair stand for all sacrifice.

verses.translation_literal: The sacrifices of God [are] a broken spirit; a heart broken and crushed, O God, you do not despise.
verses.translation_dramatic: The sacrifice that God accepts is a broken spirit. A heart that is broken, a heart crushed to powder, that, O God, you will not look down on, you will not turn from with scorn.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the verse that the psalm is remembered for. It uses the vocabulary of the altar and turns it inward: the 'sacrifices of God' are not bulls but a spirit that is broken. The Hebrew has three words of breaking, nishbarah, nishbar and nidkeh, 'broken', 'broken', 'crushed'. The KJV varies them into 'broken' and 'contrite', which is the language of later theology. Nidkeh is the word for something pounded fine, as in grinding; there is nothing polite about it.

Radak says that the Lord despises the sacrifice when the heart has not been broken; he does not despise the heart when no sacrifice is there. Ibn Ezra puts it in one phrase: repentance is as precious as the sacrifices of God. Malbim, writing in the nineteenth century, reads spirit and heart as two parts of the inner person, one that imagines and one that desires. The final verb, tivzeh, 'despise', is the same word used of Esau despising his birthright: contempt, not just rejection.

philological_notes.note: Niphal participle, 'broken'. The same root is repeated in the next phrase for the heart, so the broken spirit and broken heart are one image told twice.
'Crushed', pounded fine. The English 'contrite' comes from Latin, not from the Hebrew image of grinding.
'Despise, hold in contempt', stronger than 'reject'.

verses.translation_literal: Do good in your favour to Zion; you will build the walls of Jerusalem.
verses.translation_dramatic: And in your goodwill, do good to Zion. Rebuild her. Raise up the walls of Jerusalem again.
verses.directors_commentary:
The mood changes without warning: from the single penitent to the whole city. For an audience that knew Jerusalem only with its walls in ruins, or in the fear of it, this is the prayer of the exile; for one that thought of David, it is the city he had taken and not yet fortified. The commentators split on this. Rashi reads the walls as the Temple that Solomon would build. Ibn Ezra quotes a Spanish sage who thought the last two verses were added by a pious man in Babylon, since Zion was not yet known as the chosen place in David's time. Radak says that they are David's prophecy of the Temple's destruction and rebuilding.

'In your favour' (birtzonkha) is the word that governs the whole verse, ratzon, the same root as 'be pleased with' in verse 18. Where the offering did not please, the city will. The second verb, tivneh, is an imperfect that can be a wish or a confident 'you will build'; KJV 'build thou' and YLT 'thou dost build' take opposite sides. Zion is the sacred hill and Jerusalem the city around it: Malbim says Zion gets goodness from God's will, Jerusalem gets walls.

philological_notes.note: 'In your favour, by your goodwill', a noun from the root of 'be pleased with' in verse 18; the verse sets God's pleasure in the city against his displeasure at the offering.
An imperfect that can mean 'build!' or 'you will build'. Readers differ whether it is a wish or an assurance.
City walls, the protection of a town. Malbim contrasts the outer walls of Jerusalem with the inner presence of God at Zion.

verses.translation_literal: Then you will delight in sacrifices of righteousness, burnt offering and whole offering; then they will offer up on your altar young bulls.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then you will take delight in the sacrifices of righteousness, in the burnt offering and the whole offering. Then bulls will go up on your altar, and the smoke will rise.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two 'then's, 'az', frame the verse like a drumbeat: when the city and the heart are mended, the altar will be right again. The same verb for desire (chafetz) that was denied in verse 18 now returns with a positive subject. The sacrifices that God did not want from a sinner he will want from a people who are just. Metzudat David says that in that day the land will be full of knowledge and no one will need to bring sin-offerings, only freewill peace offerings and burnt offerings.

'Sacrifices of righteousness' is a phrase the KJV renders literally, but 'burnt offering and whole burnt offering' is a doubling that English cannot sort out: olah and kalil. Radak takes them as one thing said twice; Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion take kalil as the priest's grain offering, burned whole (Lev 6:16). 'Young bulls' (parim) is the biggest and most expensive sacrificial animal; the KJV 'bullocks' is an older English word for them. Radak notes that bulls stand for the whole range of offerings.

philological_notes.note: 'Sacrifices of righteousness': offerings brought rightly and by the just. Ibn Ezra identifies them as the peace offerings; Meiri takes them as offerings without hypocrisy.
'Whole', something burned entirely. Radak sees a synonym for olah; Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion see the priest's grain offering.
Young bulls, the largest animals offered. Radak says the bull stands for sin-offerings and peace-offerings together, and that the same holds for lambs.
